question: Can one recover a distribution-uniform, finite-sample and high-probability analogue of the asymptotic Fisher-information theory for one-dimensional location MLE?

key_findings.claim: Unsmoothed Fisher information can be arbitrarily misleading at finite sample size.
key_findings.evidence: A fine sawtooth perturbation can greatly increase density derivatives and Fisher information while remaining statistically unresolvable until enough samples align the teeth. A tiny remote spike can give infinite Fisher information and lure finite-sample MLE toward the spike even when it is not observed.

key_findings.claim: Adding matched Gaussian noise to the samples and known model yields a near-Gaussian local MLE guarantee governed by smoothed Fisher information.
key_findings.evidence: Algorithm 1 perturbs each observation by N(0,r^2), convolves the known density by the same Gaussian, and returns any empirical-score root in a supplied uncertainty interval. Under explicit relations among r, interval width, n and delta, every root has error within 1+o(1) of sqrt(2 log(1/delta)/(n I_r)).

anchors.section: Explicit local theorem and proof sketch

key_findings.claim: A quantile-localization stage removes the need for an externally supplied location interval.
key_findings.evidence: Algorithm 2 uses an adaptively chosen empirical quantile to construct a confidence interval, selects a smoothing radius proportional to a vanishing factor times the interquartile range, and invokes local smoothed MLE. Its theorem provides the same high-probability form with I at the selected radius.

key_findings.claim: The upper bound is matched, for Gaussian-smoothed densities, by a high-probability two-point lower bound up to 1+o(1).
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1.3 shows no estimator can distinguish two shifts separated by twice approximately sqrt(2 log(1/delta)/(n I_r)) with success 1-delta under its asymptotic regime, sharpening standard KL/Hellinger arguments that would lose constants.

key_findings.claim: The empirical evidence supports the smoothing tradeoff but is confined to one engineered one-dimensional distribution.
key_findings.evidence: On a Laplace body plus a narrow mass-0.001 Gaussian spike, the MSE-optimal smoothing radius falls with n. At n=500, 0.05-smoothed MLE beats unsmoothed MLE, the empirical mean and a Lee-Valiant estimator; at n=3000, unsmoothed MLE is typically sharper while smoothing improves tails.

method.core_idea: Replace raw Fisher information by the Fisher information after an n-dependent Gaussian smoothing that suppresses statistically inaccessible fine-scale density structure.
method.mechanism: Convolve the known location-family density with N(0,r^2), add matching independent noise to observations, locate a score root, prove uniform concentration and local score sign control, bootstrap a global interval with quantiles, and prove a tight high-probability shifted-pair lower bound.
assumptions: The full one-dimensional noise density is known up to translation.
Samples are i.i.d. and the shift is the only unknown parameter.
The high-probability asymptotic regime has n much larger than log(1/delta), with additional explicit smoothing conditions.
The lower bound fixes the smoothed density parameter r^2 I_r as delta tends to zero.
The algorithm can compute the smoothed score, Fisher information/quantiles and a score root sufficiently accurately.

techniques.role: Removes density features too fine or too rare for finite n while keeping a valid known location model.
Defines the effective finite-sample information scale.
Avoids requiring a unique global likelihood maximum in the local theorem.
Constructs the initial interval for a global estimator.
Obtains the Gaussian tail constant instead of only a constant-factor minimax bound.

evaluations.setting: Arbitrary one-dimensional known location density under theorem conditions.
evaluations.result: Local and global smoothed MLE achieve approximately sqrt(2 log(1/delta)/(n I_r)) with distribution-independent correction terms.
evaluations.baseline: Classical asymptotic MLE/Cramer-Rao theory using unsmoothed I.

evaluations.metric: Two-shift testing separation at success probability 1-delta.
evaluations.result: No estimator improves the proposed accuracy scale by more than a 1+o(1) factor in the stated regime.
evaluations.baseline: Standard KL or Hellinger two-point bounds that lose constants.

evaluations.setting: Laplace density with a small narrow remote Gaussian spike, n from 50 to 5,000.
evaluations.metric: MSE and empirical error distributions over smoothing radii.
evaluations.result: Intermediate smoothing wins below the spike-observation threshold; near-zero smoothing becomes best for typical error after the spike is routinely observed, while positive smoothing can retain better tails.
evaluations.baseline: Unsmoothed MLE, empirical mean and Lee-Valiant sub-Gaussian mean estimator.

limitations: The density shape is assumed exactly known; model misspecification and estimating f from data are outside the main theorem.
The result is one-dimensional, and the original guarantee does not cover vector translations.
The clean 1+o(1) statement is a joint high-probability asymptotic, not a simple small-n constant bound for every delta.
The selected smoothing radius is implicit/conservative and requires distributional quantities such as IQR and smoothed information.
Algorithm 1 assumes an uncertainty interval and returns a score root rather than solving all computational issues of nonconvex global likelihood.
The lower-bound proof is described as ad hoc and tied to Gaussian-smoothed distributions.
Only one synthetic spiked-Laplace example is evaluated; no real-data or misspecified-model experiment is included.
Random smoothing intentionally discards fine-scale information that could become useful at a different n or target failure probability.
failure_modes: Using raw Fisher information predicts impossible finite-n accuracy from unresolved sawteeth or rare spikes.
Smoothing is too small and MLE overfits a high-density feature absent from the sample.
Smoothing is too large and destroys useful information or adds dominant variance.
The chosen delta changes the optimal tail-oriented radius, but a radius tuned for MSE is reused.
A wrong density model makes matched score roots biased despite nominal concentration.
Numerical score-root selection falls outside the certified interval or fails on a nonsmooth approximation.
reusable_insights: Finite-sample information should be scale-aware: blur density structure below the resolution supported by n and delta.
Stress-test asymptotic estimators with fine oscillations and rare high-density components.
Separate typical-risk tuning from tail-risk tuning because their optimal smoothing may differ.
Pair a sharp estimator with a matching high-probability lower bound rather than quoting variance-only Cramer-Rao limits.
Use localization to turn a globally irregular likelihood into a tractable local score problem.
When extending to learned densities, include sample splitting and smoothing-selection uncertainty explicitly.
open_questions: Can an adaptive data-driven radius achieve the same guarantee without knowing f exactly?
How robust is smoothed MLE to density misspecification or contaminated samples?
Can sharp nonasymptotic constants replace the remaining o(1) regime restrictions?
Which multivariate information geometry yields a practical high-dimensional analogue?
Can the tight two-point technique be generalized into a reusable divergence inequality?
Does cross-validated smoothing retain certified tail guarantees?

competitive_landscape.title: High-dimensional Location Estimation via Norm Concentration for Subgamma Vectors
competitive_landscape.difference: The successor extends smoothed-information location estimation to high dimensions and improves the one-dimensional constant-failure regime; it explicitly notes that this paper's radius need not vanish for fixed delta.

competitive_landscape.title: Finite-Sample Symmetric Mean Estimation with Fisher Information Rate
competitive_landscape.difference: That work estimates the center of an unknown symmetric density using kernel-density ideas; the reviewed paper knows f exactly up to shift and can therefore state a cleaner location-family MLE result.

competitive_landscape.title: Nonparametric Estimation of the Fisher Information and Its Applications
competitive_landscape.difference: Cao et al. estimate location Fisher information itself from samples under regularity conditions, including after Gaussian contamination; the reviewed paper assumes the density known and uses smoothed information to certify a shift estimator.

competitive_landscape.title: U-statistics of growing order and sub-Gaussian mean estimators with sharp constants
competitive_landscape.difference: Minsker targets sharp sub-Gaussian mean estimation with only moment assumptions; smoothed MLE exploits a known distribution shape to improve the variance scale from distribution variance to inverse smoothed Fisher information.

novelty_assessment: The paper gives a compelling scale-aware repair of classical MLE theory: Gaussian-smoothed Fisher information captures finite-n resolvability, and the upper/lower tail constants nearly match. The result is technically strong but narrow—known one-dimensional densities and a high-probability asymptotic regime—and later work already improves constant-delta behavior and dimension.
